Creativity Techniques · U3 Development Techniques and Solutions

1 · Make it rough, make it early

A rough prototype is a question in material form. Make the smallest version that can teach you something.

A rough thing can answer a question that a polished thing hides.

(Tao of Creativity)

Image: Early-1900s photograph of Gaudí's hanging model for the Colonia Güell church: strings loaded with small sacks of weight hang from the ceiling, with paper draped over them to show the inverted form.

Antoni Gaudí's hanging string-and-weight model for the Colonia Güell church, photographed c. 1908 · Unknown photographer (Gaudí workshop, c. 1908) · Public domain · Source

Creativity Techniques · U3 Development Techniques and Solutions

2 · Defer judgement

Protect a short space for variation before you decide what works. Then judge with a named criterion.

Image: A page from Beethoven's 1812 sketchbook: hurried ink notation across many staves as themes for the Seventh Symphony are tried out.

Beethoven's sketchbook for the Seventh Symphony, 1812 · Ludwig van Beethoven (sketchbook); Daderot (photograph, public-domain dedication) · Public domain · Source

Creativity Techniques · U3 Development Techniques and Solutions

3 · Iterate with an exit

Write the test before the next version. Stop when the test is answered.

Creativity Techniques · U3 Development Techniques and Solutions

4 · Sketch to think

Three quick arrangements can show relationships that one polished drawing hides.

Sketching enables exploration of the problem space and the solution space to proceed together.

(Cross 2006, 46)

Course diagram · Koch triangle · #5cc4358a9bdb · Original course SVG

Creativity Techniques · U3 Development Techniques and Solutions

5 · Open the solution space

Reframe an unclear brief as two or three questions. Make one small response to each.

(Beghetto and Karwowski 2025, 1)

Creativity Techniques · U3 Development Techniques and Solutions

Exercise 1 · Same problem, three entry points

Keep one D1 problem. Start each of three rough sketches from a different named entry point. Do not polish. Compare how the entry point steered the path (de Bono 1970, 27; Cross 2006, 93).

Save the problem, three entry points, three scans, and one sentence on what each entry point made possible.

Image: An early-19th-century watercolour design sheet showing three chairs side by side, each with a differently curved back and patterned seat.

An early-19th-century design sheet with three chairs with curved backs · Anonymous designer (early 19th century); The Metropolitan Museum of Art (CC0) · CC0 1.0 · Source

Creativity Techniques · U3 Development Techniques and Solutions

Exercise 2 · Delay judgement, then checkpoint and exit

Protect a short delay of judgement on one version (de Bono 1970, 30). Write one testable question, revise once, and stop when the test is answered.

Save before/after, the deferred-judgement note, the test question, the checkpoint, and the exit decision.
